title: Buddy Petit, the Decatur Street job, Sidney Arodin and wartime
summary: Lee praises Buddy Petit's playing, describes a mixed band on Decatur Street with Sidney Arodin and Lazy River, and why he avoided shipyard work in the war.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: How did Buddy Petit play? Buddy Petit played the semi, just like Bunk.

I couldn't tell the difference between him and Buddy, him and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that really knocked me out. He really, he really, none of our comments playing like between Buddy and Bunk. Buddy Petit was the corner player that had a great big tune and a beautiful soul. And he played with a great drive. He didn't play many high notes, but he didn't need to make no high notes. The way that guy played in the scales was everything. He played with really, he didn't need to make no high notes. So Buddy was very good. So Buddy taking a light to me, he said, kid, he say, he called me then Little Lee. Everybody used to call me Little Lee. He said, Little Lee, you really knocked me out. He said, you're doing good. He said, you put me in my old bunk. I said, well that's my man, that's the guy I wanted, that's the guy like to play like Buddy was Bunk. So he said, that's the guy I come by too, Bunk. He said, Bunk and Joe Johnson, that was the man that knocked me out. So I went to the garden and I go to work. That time on a place they called on Decatur Street. It was run by a little Spanish guy. Decatur, it was on Decatur's out there around by the French market. And it was about three players. We had a white guitar and a white piano player, the boy by the name was Sidney Adrian, but later recorded with me with this story, a story band I think I said. So Sidney Adrian and his guitar player, he was an unknown guitar, I'd like to remember his name, but he was a very good guitar player. He worked piano and drum. He was just a picked up band. That's why I say old New Orleans had mixed bands, I think before they ever thought of that, and nobody paid a bit of attention to it. So Sidney Adrian and I would play together. That's where Sidney Adrian used to play this number. What's this number he composed when he sold it to Carmichael? Lazy River. Lazy River. Lazy River. He used to play it and mug it every time he got drunk. He used to play, because he got that inspiration, he used to go sit on the river every morning and blow his clarinet and look at the river and then the river was kind of lazy that time of the morning coming into Carmichael. He used to play that piece, Lazy River. And I used to play it with him. I was way back there before Lazy River ever think that I would, when I seen the musical Lazy River, I learned Lazy River. All I did was sit in his piece right away. So Bill, we played in this little job, then the war was on. The 1917 war was on. And made little things different, musicians, half of them was, because they had a lot of work or fight. Some of them was working, but I never did work, because I always knew all the little hiding places outside the district where you could go, I could go hide in my corner and play. So, I stayed awake. Well, one time I did try to wake. Joe Lindsey and Louis Armstrong carried me, we all made up, Louis was waking out there, and they all made up their mind to go to wake. Louis was to go to wake, and they carried me out there, and I seen how hard the wake was before I could start, and I slipped off. What sort of a job was it? Oh man, it was rolling cement up there, with a ship building, building ships, building ships. And I was, shucks, I didn't get it for a $50 a day, I didn't want no part of it, because I still love my own. I didn't want to stay away from that long, that long way from my corner. So, I got away from that way.
